identity.title: New or progressive back pain in a patient with known cancer (or age >50, night pain, weight loss)

technique.how: Ask specifically about any prior cancer diagnosis (including remote and 'cured'), and characterize the pain: onset, progression, night or rest pain, thoracic location, unexplained weight loss, and duration over one month. Then screen for cord/cauda equina symptoms: leg weakness, gait change, saddle numbness, urinary retention or incontinence.
technique.prerequisites: Reliable history or collateral; access to oncology records if the patient is unsure.

interpretation.positive_finding: A prior cancer history is the only red flag shown to substantially raise the probability of spinal malignancy: post-test probability 7% in primary care and 33% in an ED cohort. With new neurological symptoms treat as possible metastatic cord compression.
interpretation.negative_finding: No cancer history makes spinal malignancy unlikely in primary care (prevalence <1%), but minor red flags (age >50, weight loss, failure to improve) are weakly informative and cannot exclude it.
interpretation.pitfalls: Age >50, night pain and weight loss have high false-positive rates when used alone. Sensitivity of 'history of cancer' is modest, so its absence does not clear a patient with progressive or thoracic pain.
interpretation.changes_what: Positive: same-day whole-spine MRI (urgent if any neurological deficit) and dexamethasone per local pathway; negative: routine care unless other red flags accumulate.

sources.citation: Downie A, Williams CM, Henschke N, et al. Red flags to screen for malignancy and fracture in patients with low back pain: systematic review. BMJ 2013;347:f7095.
Henschke N, Maher CG, Ostelo RW, de Vet HC, Macaskill P, Irwig L. Red flags to screen for malignancy in patients with low-back pain. Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2013;2:CD008686.
Deyo RA, Diehl AK. Cancer as a cause of back pain: frequency, clinical presentation, and diagnostic strategies. J Gen Intern Med 1988;3:230-238.
Deyo RA, Rainville J, Kent DL. What can the history and physical examination tell us about low back pain? JAMA 1992;268:760-765.

safety_scope.do_not_use_when: Not a substitute for a neurological examination; do not let an absent cancer history delay imaging when there are motor, sensory or sphincter symptoms.
safety_scope.escalation_warning: Back pain plus leg weakness, saddle anaesthesia or urinary retention in a cancer patient is metastatic cord compression until proven otherwise: emergency MRI and steroids.
safety_scope.interobserver_note: Red-flag questions are reproducible but their reported accuracy varies with how 'history of cancer' is defined (any vs. active) and with setting prevalence.

extraction_notes: No sens/spec/LR could be verified for 'history of cancer': they appear only in Downie 2013 Fig 4 (image) and in the non-OA Cochrane (Henschke 2013) and JAMA RCE (Deyo 1992) tables, so estimates are empty. Post-test probabilities visible in the OA BMJ text (PMC3898572, Results, 'Red flags for spinal malignancy' paragraph): 'When present, "history of cancer" suggests a post-test probability of 7% (95% confidence interval 3% to 16%) in primary care' (Deyo & Diehl 1988, 1975 walk-in patients, prevalence 0.66%) 'and 33% (22% to 46%) in the emergency setting' (Reinus 1998, ED radiograph cohort). Did not convert these to an LR because the figure's pre-test line (0.5%) is a nominal setting prevalence, not the study prevalence. Deyo 1988 abstract lists prior cancer as significantly associated with malignancy but gives no accuracy numbers; Deyo 1992 RCE abstract is empty in PubMed (title/authors confirmed). All PMIDs confirmed via tools/pubmed.py fetch.
